Overall, it was a great episode. I agree with some critics that the pacing was sometimes a little quick and that the parts with the narration were pretty cheap, but I still thought it was a great send off for Matt Smith while tying up most of the loose plot threads of the previous seasons.

I know this might be profane of me to say, but I was actually much more moved by Smith's Regeneration than Tennant's. Tennant's was sad, but I was never actually close to crying. Smith's last farewell did manage to hit me in the gut a couple of times. I look forward to the continuing adventures of Peter Capaldi and his strangely colored kidneys.

I hate to repeat what I said in the thread of the Day of the Doctor, but this episode made me dislike Moffat even more. I don't want to be a downer, but I had a really hard time getting past the pacing issues and the fact that certain plot elements were brought up so quickly and brushed aside with so little care that I felt like the story didn't care about itself. Why was his regeneration glossed over so quickly? Tennant got such a beautiful moment of getting to see all the companions and people he had affected, whereas Smith only got to see Amy and not a single other side character that he had interacted with. I felt like Smith's Doctor deserved more than what the episode gave him. The episode was fine, but that pacing just slayed it.

Cinematography was nice, though.

posts.cooked:
He was on the planet for like 900 years, and really the only important thing going on is a war, which the best way to show is how they did it, with little individual highlights here and there. A lot of the plot elements that were brought up were explanations to mysteries and questions that had been asked since series 5. All of the important things we actually needed to know were shown to us in the episode.

Matt's regeneration wasn't glossed over. He got to use new energy to blow up a Dalek spaceship, then got to give a dramatic speech to Clara, and then still got to have a touching moment with Karen Gillan. Honestly, the moment with Karen had a lot more impact then Tennant's trips to his companions. For one thing, we already had a tying of loose knots so to speak with season 4's finale, we didn't really need it again with End of Time.

Amy hasn't been gone that long but she is the Matt Smith companion. Rory is awesome but his whole plotline is tied in to Amy, and having him there too would probably be a bit redundant. You don't really need the other important side characters because River already got a send off in Name of the Doctor and most of the other ones are probably going to make appearances in the future.

The moment with Amy was very poignant and wasn't longer than it needed to be. Smith's regeneration wasn't longer than it needed to be. In a lot of ways Tennant's was overdramatic and bloated. Smith's was sad but still hopeful and optimistic for the future which is more interesting and more in the general spirt of the show.

All in all, I thought it was a great send off for Matt and a great way to kick off Capaldi's tenure. I love Moffat's style an look forward to seeing what he pulls out next.

posts.name: Braithwhite
posts.cooked:
io9 had a lovely article about how each Doctor's final episode kind of sums up their entire character.  For me, It felt like an appropriate sendoff for Matt Smith, in that it was hectic and glossed over some of the important bits (wait, he has a new best friend/lover that he's known forever that we're only now meeting?  AGAIN?)...but thats been a key component of his character since Amy Pond's departure. Its one of the reasons that it felt so right that she made a cameo at the end to take him away.

For me, it felt like the doctor died when Amy couldn't be saved.  they were tied together, and without her he drifted.  There were adventures, but many of them happened without us (the audience).  He was starting to pull himself back together with Clara, but it felt like the 11th doctor had lost his steady anchor.  Clara is a good companion, but he held her at a distance- dropping her off between adventures, "saving" her by sending her off, and keeping her at arm's length.  

I can't deny that the show itself had pacing problems- but I didn't mind the narration, because to me that's what the Doctor's life WAS without Pond. He'd gotten more withdrawn and fatalistic, and the only way anyone could know him anymore was from the outside- even those that he flirted with or helped.

Amy Pond, and his adventures and interactions with her was his entire life.  And when he saw her again, he could let go and be someone else- hopefully one who can let people in again.

I'v never seen an episode of this show in my life up until my sister made me watch this episode. So, as someone who is not emotionally tied to the series, here were my impressions:

Sending Clara away multiple times took away the impact (for me) of doing it in the first place. Kinda a "fool me once" type deal. Wasn't quite sure her presence was at all needed aboard the church ship thingy from a narative standpoint when the lady turned into a dalek. It could have been a much more profound moment if the first time she saw him again was an old man. 

If they did it that way, they could have cut down the narrated montoges by half (which were all pretty unnessesary. do they happen offten on the series?). Those scenes contributed in no small degree to the pacing critique.

The crack in the wall. Didn't clara answer them? Wasnt the whole point that answering it would bring them back? They just stopped trying? If there was already war, why not just bring them back? Granted these all stem from my ignorance of the show, but it felt a little contrived? 

All that being said, the show admitedly had a lot of charm about it, and it certainly caught my interest.

And the snowy statue things remind me of the ghosts in Bowers Castle.

posts.name: Nielzabub
posts.cooked:
Time of the Doctor is not a great first episode. Sort of like how the end of season 4 and End of Time was Davies giving himself one last large hurrah, he felt a need to give himself two hurrahs for some reason, Time of the Doctor was Steven Moffat tying up all the plotlines he's been creating over the past few years so that the new Doctor can start with a mostly clean slate. He's got the plot line of trying to find and bring Gallifrey peacefuly back into the universe, but other than that he won't have to deal with too much past baggage.

For me, personally, the revelation of the crack was pretty awesome. I had been wondering for a while why the Silence blew up his TARDIS to up the universe they were trying to protect. There's no way to know what all the Timelords can do on the other side of the crack. They may be able to send things through like regeneration energy or maybe other small or light objects, but they may not be able to bring in their whole planet from the other side.

The best episodes to start with continuity wise are either Rose, the first episode of the reboot in 2005, or the eleventh hour, Matt Smith's first full episode and the start of Steven Moffat's tenure as head writer and show runner.

The regeneration where Smith blows up the Dalek ships didn't count for me. I found that to be extremely over-the-top and silly. The timelords just gave him the ability to do that? What about Strax, Madam Vastra, and Jenny Flint? They made quite a few appearances, no goodbye to them?

I'd have preferred it if the episode didn't take place over 900 years. I've never been a huge fan of time-lapses that are just summed up with some lazy narration. If they had fixed the pacing, this probably would have been a much better episode.

I've long ago stopped trying to critique Doctor Who. I've learned it is science fantasy, not science fiction, and I need to not expect it to be logical, consistent, or realistic. My spouse loves the characters and enjoys the show greatly, for which I am very thankful, but for me it's just okay.

On your points, evandan, because Moffat's still running the show, I imagine we're going to see more of those characters, so we (as the audience) will not need a goodbye - and in Tennant's case, I really looked at those moments as the audience's goodbyes as much as Tennant's.

For the regeneration destroying ships, I extrapolated that this regeneration was different, that the Time Lords actually gave him a full new set of regenerations, and the power output of that was huge. This was mostly just me making up a justification, so don't read into it, but it's one of the approaches I've taken to make the show make sense for myself.

The 900 years is, for me, more of an issue because there's no way a society under attack for that long would not advance technologically in ways to improve their own defensive and offensive capabilities, even with the Doctor there. But it is what it is…

Mezike:

Those rubber men with the shrimp heads were more reminiscent of the worst of the shows budget monsters (Confessssss - yeah, okay).

They were used to much greater effect in their earlier episodes… At least I thought they were.

posts.cooked:
The whole 12 regeneration limit was always kind of a dumb idea. It was done with the 4th Doctor to create a confict for the Master who had run out of regenerations. The Master reappeared in season 3 with a complete new set of regenerations with no explanation other than the Timelords revived him. There is some precedence for Timelord magic.

Tennant's regeneration was very goofy. I liked it, but was there any real reason for the TARDIS to be destroyed? Eccleston regenerated just fine in the TARDIS with no damage done at all. The explosive destroy the Daleks with regeneration energy was silly, but so what? Doctor Who has always been silly. We need to stop pretending that the Davies era wasn't also stupid. The Davies era was completely silly what with the whole Doctor absorbs psychic energy which somehow makes him young again and gives him momentary super powers at the end of season 3. How does that work? Psychic energy, that's how it works, I guess. At least Time of the Doctor had some genuine emotion behind its silliness.

Clara getting sent away multiple times probably hurt her character development a little, but the Doctor has done this to his companions before. In season 1 he sent Rose away when there was danger. If he's in a situation he doesn't think he can win, he'll do what he can to save his companions, and this is not a character trait Clara was familiar with, so maybe now she'll be more used to it in her adventures with Capaldi.

I'll agree that the narration was the weakest part of the episode, but it kept the viewer from having to view the more repetetive parts of the plot and just move on with the actual story of the episode, and so I can live with it.

Like Rabit said, there wasn't a need for a really long drawn out goodbye to every companion because we'll probably be seeing most of them again anyway.

posts.name: Envisioner
posts.cooked:
Nielzabub:

but so what? Doctor Who has always been silly.

That is a pretty big what.  It is the biggest single flaw with the show, the fact that it makes only a tenuous effort to make sense, and constantly undermines its own integrity as a result of the ever-changing creative team.  Imagine what a mess SOTM would be if new people took it over starting in Infernal Relics and rewrote all the continuity, so that now Tachyon was actually a space alien from the planet Speedulon while Tempest was really Legacy's undersea clone-brother with a lightning-variant AZ suit implanted under his skin which turned him green.  SOTM retains its quality largely as a result of being kept under the control of its original designers.  If the people who keep taking over Dr. Who and reinventing it would instead have created original shows, similar to Dr. Who but with their own continuities that don't constantly reinvent the past of a profitable franchise, the result would likely be substantially better.

posts.cooked: I think Moffat has done a great job at keeping with the continuity. My point was that his silliness isn't really any less than Davies's silliness. It's different, but not any worse. The reason Doctor Who has been able to survive for 50 years is because of its changing staff and dynamic nature. It can evolve and be relevant to any era. Silliness is just fine if it works in the context of the story being told, and most of the time it does. I do not think the show's integrity has ever really been compromised. It has always been a silly soft sci-fi show about a man with a magic box who travles through time and space trying to make things better for everyone that he can. Despite it's many changes, the show has managed to stay true to that course and remain popular and interesting.

posts.cooked:
My thoughts aren't anything new.  Like many, I thought Tennant's goodbye was a little too drawn out and lengthy, so I thought Matt Smith's was a nice contrast.  I'm a little surprised that when he sent away Clara for the second time (right after swearing to her that he wouldn't) they didn't bring up the whole "Rule #1: The doctor lies." thing, but whatever.  Overall I liked the episode, and I thought it was an interesting explanation of the whole Trendzalore (sp?) thing.

 

As for silliness in Doctor Who, the near breaking point for me came with the whole galactic prison thing.  <SPOILER> They spent several episodes building this whole thing about this unbreakable prison, and what/who could possibly be inside.  Once he's imprisoned, how does he get out?  He basically pulls a Bill and Ted, and after he gets out, he goes back and lets himself out (via Amy Pond).  Wait what? </SPOILER>  <- Is there a way to do that on here?

 

It bothered me a lot at first, and then I just kind of got over it, but now I reference it as an example any time someone tries to get overly "technical" about Doctor Who.

posts.cooked:
Having finally watched it after being horribly ill and then on vacation, I will weigh in.

 

This is the most epic send-off any doctor has received.  Far cry from the sad lay down and swap faces that the old ones got.  

 

As to the story, I'm a fan of the old shows so all of the new stuff seems fast paced and full of glossing over things to move the story along too fast.  I thought the plot fit his character, this doctor never let himself live in the past, always his mind on where he was, the Doctor who wouldn't look back.  The regeneration energy as the most powerful weapon in existence was ridiculous, but excusable if you try hard enough, and the start of Capaldi went very well.  Every Doctor gets bombed for his regeneration openning, and everyone gets over it and moves on.

I hope Capaldi brings in a slower style that actually develops characters and has the doctor find answers by doing more than pointing a screwdriver at everything.  There are recurring characters that I don't feel like I have any idea who they are, and have a hard time caring about, in the old days you got a real good sense and attachment to characters that were only around for a story arc, or less in some cases.

Basically it was better than expected, but they still don't make them like they used to.

posts.name: Nielzabub
posts.cooked:
I think most of the characters and plot were given as much time to develop as they needed to.They're not exactly in depth characters, but they're interesting and entertaining. The fast paced nature of the narrative also perfectly complemented Matt Smith's portrayel of the Doctor. the only characters in the Davies era other than the Doctor that I felt particularly attached to were Donna and Captain Jack. I've pretty much loved every side character introduced in the most recent era. Craig and the Pasternoster Gang are very fun and vibrant characters, and although there were times Amy needed to be slapped, I still found her story arc much more engaging and emotional than the Tween puppy love Rose had with the Doctor. I think Clara is a bit underrated as a companion. She's the only traveller in the new Who that hasn't just entirely abandoned her life to travel with the Doctor. She's kept a very clear line between her real life and her adventures. The romance angle was slightly forced and unnecessary, but I think it will be interesting to see how that changes now that the Doctor is an old man.

That being said, I do think this is a good time for a stylistic change, and I can definitely understand the want and need for a slower pacing. You can go only go so big before you need to start going small again.
